item.title: Swiss Stock Exchange: Volumes Fall in July
item.description: Trading activity on the Swiss market fell by 10.4% compared to June, but the number of transactions rose by 2.3%.

The figure released today by the management company SIX shows a contraction that affected all asset classes, albeit with different intensities. The biggest setback was recorded by ETF funds, whose trading fell by 24% month-on-month. On the other hand, the decline in equities was smaller, limiting the decline to 8%.

item.title: Cars in Switzerland: decline in July, BYD electric boom
item.description: Registrations fell by 3.2% in July, but electrification continues. BYD overtakes Tesla in the Swiss electric car market.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - New car sales down 3.2% in July 2026. - Total of 19,000 new registrations in Switzerland. - Alternative propulsion systems account for 76% of the market share. - BYD overtakes Tesla in electric car sales.
## Key Facts - **What**: Trend of the Swiss automotive market - When: July 2026 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Auto-Switzerland - Amount: 3.2% decrease compared to the previous July
The Swiss car market slowed down in July 2026, following a brief recovery in June. According to data provided by the importers' association Auto-Switzerland, 19,000 fresh cars were put on the road, a decrease of 3.2% compared to the same period of the previous year. Despite this decline in overall volumes, the transition to greener engines continues to consolidate, profoundly influencing the choices of Swiss consumers.
### The growth of the electricity sector The detailed analysis for July reveals that alternative powertrains, which include electric, hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles, achieved an overall market share of 76%, up sharply from 68% in July 2025. At the heart of this dynamic is the regular hybrid segment, which holds a 37% share, up from 35% a year earlier. The purely electric sector also shows considerable vigor, reaching 26% of the market, with 4500 cars registered and a growth of 20% on an annual basis. At the same time, plug-in hybrid stands at 14%, compared to 12% previously. On the contrary, traditional engines are losing ground: petrol cars are down to 18% from 24% last year, while diesel vehicles are down to 6% from the original 8%. This shift towards environmentally friendly technologies is the direct result of an aggressive commercial strategy by manufacturers, who offer a wide range in different price ranges, while ensuring improved ranges and reduced operating costs. The director of Auto-Switzerland, Thomas Rücker, emphasizes that this electrification is a gradual process, actively supported by importers despite the economic challenges, which remain, according to the executive, "immense". Analyzing the cumulative data for the first seven months of 2026, the picture of the Swiss market appears more complex. Overall, 135,500 cars were registered, an increase of 2.1% compared to the same period in 2025. This reflects the resilience of the sector over the long term, despite monthly fluctuations. Looking at the specific volumes by type of propulsion, it can be seen that hybrids reached 49,600 units (+2%), while electric cars stood at 32,900 units (+20%). On the contrary, classic engines suffered: petrol vehicles fell to 28,600 units (-13%) and diesels to 7600 (-23%). Plug-in hybrids closed the period with 16,900 registrations (+21%). Of particular note is the increase in the share of 4x4 vehicles, from 50% to 53%, confirming a Swiss consumer preference for all-wheel drive.
### The challenge between BYD and Tesla Perhaps the most striking figure of this period is the rise of the Chinese manufacturer BYD. In the brand comparison, BYD sold 3300 vehicles between January and July, marking a growth of 1197% compared to 300 units in the same period of 2025. Tesla, while maintaining a growth of 2% over the seven months, experienced a decidedly difficult month of July with only 100 cars sold (-78%), against BYD's 600. This competition reflects a profound shift in Swiss market preferences, where new international players are rapidly eroding market share from established leaders. Volkswagen remains the leading brand with 15,300 cars sold, followed by Skoda (12,900), BMW (11,200) and Mercedes (10,700). Regulatory pressure remains a sticking point: Auto-Switzerland continues its battle against overregulation, calling on politicians to improve the regulatory framework to strengthen the engine of the economy. Importers remain focused on optimizing the offer, trying to meet the needs of customers who are increasingly attentive to operating costs and environmental performance, in a macroeconomic context that requires constant adaptation and technological innovation to maintain competitiveness on national markets.

item.title: Publibike switches to a UK investor
item.description: The Swiss bicycle rental company Publibike is majority-owned by British investor Visionedgeone.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Publibike switches to Visionedgeone - Markus Bacher remains CEO and minority shareholder - Visionedgeone owns Inurba Mobility
## Key Facts - **What**: Majority transfer of Publibike to Visionedgeone - When: July 30, 2024 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Visionedgeone - Amount: Not specified
BERN - Swiss bicycle rental company Publibike is passing a majority stake to British investor Visionedgeone. Current CEO Markus Bacher will retain leadership of the company and will remain a minority shareholder. The news was reported on Monday by the CH-Media Group's "Schweiz heute" portal, after the same company had already announced the change of ownership on July 30 on its website. The price of the transaction was not disclosed.
With the transaction, the current shareholders are selling their shares, with the exception of Bacher. Among those retiring is Bern entrepreneur Thomas Binggeli, founder and owner of Thömus, who has said he wants to return to focusing fully on his other activities.
Visionedgeone has made a long-term commitment, for at least five years, Bacher indicated. The investor already owns Inurba Mobility, a bike sharing operator active in several European countries including France, Finland and Poland. The aim is to exploit possible synergies in terms of technology, distribution and management.
Under the new ownership, Publibike intends to strengthen investments in the fleet, services and technology, as well as expand the offer to other Swiss cities and municipalities. Currently, the company operates around 10,500 bicycles and e-bikes in around 120 cities and municipalities spread across ten cantons, with customers including Zurich, Bern, Basel, Biel and Aarau.
The public sector partly supports the business through annual contributions and guarantees to cover the deficit. Publibike was previously controlled by Swiss Post and was sold in 2022 to a group of investors led by Bacher, Binggeli and IT entrepreneur Guido Honegger. Since 2024, the company has been recording positive operating results (EBITDA), according to Bacher. ### Implications for the Swiss market
The acquisition of Publibike by Visionedgeone could lead to a strengthening of the bike sharing sector in Switzerland. With Visionedgeone's experience in several European countries, it is expected that Publibike will benefit from new technologies and better management practices. This could result in a more efficient service and greater geographical coverage, with potential new customers in other Swiss cities and municipalities.
### Synergies and innovation
The goal of leveraging technology and management synergies could lead to significant innovations in the industry. Visionedgeone, with its expertise in France, Finland, and Poland, could introduce new technology solutions that improve user experience and fleet management. This could include improvements in rental apps, more efficient charging systems for e-bikes, and new ways of distribution.
### Expansion and investment
With plans to expand its offerings to other Swiss cities and municipalities, Publibike could see a significant increase in its user base. This could lead to increased demand for bicycles and e-bikes, further stimulating the bike-sharing market. Investments in the fleet and services could also improve the quality of service offered, making Publibike an even more attractive choice for consumers.
### Public support
Public sector support through annual contributions and guarantees to cover the deficit is a crucial factor in Publibike's success. With the new ownership, Publibike is expected to continue to receive this support, ensuring the financial sustainability of the company and allowing it to keep prices affordable for users.

## In brief - Switzerland has been included in a list of 60 countries deemed to have failed to introduce or effectively enforce a ban on the import of goods produced with forced labour. - The US has imposed an additional duty of 12.5% on countries that do not have an import ban on products made using forced labour. - The Swiss government has rejected the accusations, saying that its approach combines regulation, mandatory risk assessments promoted by the private sector and international cooperation.
## Key Facts - **What**: Switzerland has been included in a list of 60 countries deemed to have failed to introduce or effectively enforce a ban on the import of goods produced with forced labour. - When: June 2, 2023. - Where: Switzerland. - Who: United States. - Amount: Additional duty of 12.5%.
On March 12, 2023, the United States announced an investigation against Switzerland under Section 301 of the US Trade Act, which concerns unfair or discriminatory trade practices. The aim was to test whether Switzerland was doing enough to prevent the import of goods produced by forced labour. The International Labour Organization defines forced labour as "any work or service extorted from a person under threat of punishment and for which the person has not volunteered himself". Punishments may include violence, intimidation, or forms of coercion such as withholding wages or confiscating passports.
The results of the US survey were released on 2 June 2023 and Switzerland was included in a list of 60 countries deemed to have failed to introduce or effectively enforce a ban on the import of goods produced with forced labour. The US trade representative said that Switzerland and the other countries concerned would not effectively combat the phenomenon and expose American producers to unfair competition.
On July 23, 2023, the US announced the imposition of an additional flat-rate duty of 12.5% on countries that, like Switzerland, do not have an import ban on products made using forced labor.
### The Swiss point of view
Forced labour is prohibited in Switzerland and the country has ratified the most important international labour and human rights conventions. However, unlike the European Union, it does not have legislation that explicitly prohibits the import of goods produced with forced labor. A draft law is currently being prepared, but it will only affect about thirty large companies. It is precisely for this reason that Switzerland is in the crosshairs of an additional tariff of 12.5%, compared to the 10% envisaged for the EU, which already has legislation on the subject.
The Swiss government has rejected accusations that the country is a sort of "free zone" for products related to forced labor. According to Bern, the approach adopted combines regulation, mandatory risk assessments promoted by the private sector and international cooperation.
"This approach focuses on preventing and combating the causes within supply chains. These approaches differ in methodology, but not in objective and effectiveness. The US industry does not suffer any damage as a result of this Swiss practice," the government said in a statement.
Economiesuisse, the umbrella association of the Swiss economy, also spoke on the subject of the private sector's responsibilities in preventing forced labour along supply chains. ### Practical implications for Swiss companies
Swiss companies, especially large ones, will face new challenges due to international pressures. Companies must ensure that their suppliers comply with human rights and international labor standards. This could lead to increased operational costs and the need to implement new policies and procedures to monitor supply chains.
### Impact on Swiss consumers
Swiss consumers could see an increase in the prices of imported products due to the new tariffs imposed by the United States. This could affect the availability and cost of consumer goods, especially for those products that are heavily dependent on imports.
### The future of Swiss supply chains
The future of Swiss supply chains will largely depend on the effectiveness of the measures taken to prevent forced labour. Companies, consumers and the Swiss government will need to work together to address this challenge and ensure that products imported into Switzerland are made under ethical and human rights conditions.
### Conclusion
The current situation underscores the importance of effective regulation and international cooperation to combat forced labor in global supply chains. Switzerland must continue to work to improve its policies and procedures to ensure that its products are produced under ethical and human rights-respecting conditions.

## In brief - Analysis of the 2026 cantonal tax rates in Switzerland. - Focus on the specific tax dynamics of the Canton of Vaud. - Differences between brackets and legitimate optimization strategies.
## Key Facts - **What**: Cantonal tax on earned income. - When: Fiscal year 2026. - Where: Switzerland, with an in-depth look at the Canton of Vaud. - Who: Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV). - Amount: Variable depending on the canton and taxable income.
The Swiss tax landscape for the year 2026 remains complex, with a division of competences that sees the Federal Tax Administration (FTA/ESTV) define the general principles, while the individual cantons retain the right to set their own rates. This cantonal autonomy generates significant differences in the overall tax burden for taxpayers. In the Canton of Vaud, as in other cantons, the system is based on income brackets that determine the progression of the tax. It is essential to underline that for cross-border workers, withholding tax is the standard method of levy, withheld directly by the employer in Switzerland. This mechanism avoids double taxation, thanks to the tax credit provided for by the EC framework of 730 in Italy. The current legislation, including the management of the New Cross-Border Workers' Agreement which came into force on 1 January 2024, defines the applicable exemptions: 7,500 euros for 'old' cross-border workers, under a transitional regime until 2033, and 10,000 euros for new hires. The double taxation agreement between Italy and Switzerland, signed on 9 December 1976, remains the fundamental pillar of this cross-border balance. The calculation of the tax does not depend on institutions such as the FSIO, which is responsible for social security, but follows the directives of the cantonal administrations. ### Cantonal tax dynamics The discrepancy between the cantons arises not only from the basic rates, but also from the municipal multipliers that are added to the cantonal tax. In the canton of Vaud, the competent authorities regularly update the tables based on the parameters defined by the FTA/ESTV. For those planning to stay or work in Switzerland in 2026, it is essential to monitor the official communications of the relevant cantonal administration, as changes can significantly affect the monthly net income. The practical analysis of cantonal taxes requires a clear understanding of the deduction mechanism. In addition to income tax, the employee is subject to compulsory social contributions: AHV/IV/EO at 5.3% for the employee, AD/AC at 1.1% (with a ceiling calculated on an income of CHF 148,200), and variable quotas for UVG (0.7–1.5%) and BVG (7–18% depending on the age group, from the age of 25). These deductions reduce the tax base, but represent a fixed cost that must be considered in the national comparison. Compared to the Italian system, which is characterised by IRPEF brackets (23% up to €28,000, 35% up to €50,000 and 43% above this threshold), the Swiss system offers greater fragmentation. ### Operational comparison For a taxpayer assessing the tax burden between different cantons, including the canton of Vaud, the comparison should not be limited to the nominal rate. Deductions for professional expenses, social security contributions and the impact of the municipal multiplier must be considered. Legitimate financial planning involves optimising these elements. For example, the choice of health insurance company (KVG) plays a crucial role: the right of option for cross-border commuters allows them to manage the insurance premium, with deductibles ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 for adults. This is not a 'health tax', but a mandatory coverage that affects the family budget. The tax impact in 2026 will also be influenced by the possible revision of the cantonal rates, which each canton decides independently. ## In brief - Tens of thousands of migrants have crossed the border into the Schengen area. - The incident is fueling political debate, even in Switzerland. - The Federal Council must introduce systematic border controls.
## Key facts - **What**: Massive influx of migrants into the Schengen area. - When: Thursday, March 17, 2023. - Where: Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, North Africa. - Who: Swiss Federal Council, Spanish Guardia Civil. - Amount: Around 49,000 arrivals in Ceuta and hundreds in Melilla.
The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa are under pressure from a massive influx of migrants. On Thursday, thousands of people reached Ceuta by swimming or walking from Morocco, thus entering the Schengen area, which also includes Switzerland. On Friday, the Spanish Guardia Civil reported 49,000 arrivals, not counting the hundreds of migrants who entered Melilla. The government has sent the army for support.
The causes are not yet fully clear. There is talk of a decision by the Spanish Supreme Court that migrants attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla by swimming cannot be turned back without further reasons. There is also speculation about a possible deliberate easing of controls by Morocco.
In Switzerland, the events in North Africa are sparking very different reactions politically.
"No one should risk their life to be protected"
Socialist National Councillor Michelle Dünki-Bättig speaks of shocking images: "People are trying to swim to a European border and dying in the attempt." She argues that the army and fences do not solve the problem; instead, they make escape routes even more dangerous. Europe needs safe and legal access routes and an effective sea rescue system.
Switzerland must also act, adds Dünki-Bättig. She calls for the reintroduction of asylum in embassies, abolished in 2012, which allowed asylum applications to be submitted at a Swiss representation abroad. The humanitarian visa, she says, is not an equivalent substitute: "No one who needs protection should have to risk their life just to apply for asylum."
"They are not refugees at all"
"What is happening is absolutely alarming," says Pascal Schmid, the SVP's asylum spokesman. "Whoever crosses the border in Ceuta is, in fact, also in Switzerland," referring to the Schengen and Dublin areas, where there are no systematic internal border controls to stop irregular migration. For this reason, he supports the request of the Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to suspend the Schengen agreement with Spain.
Schmid demands immediate measures: "The Federal Council must introduce systematic border controls immediately, as the SVP has been demanding for a long time." An "illegal mass migration" like in 2015 must be avoided at all costs, and the population must be protected from further imported crime. The democentric National Councillor and former judge also criticizes the "out-of-this-world" ruling of the Spanish court and denounces increasing legalization in the field of migration: "Intrusive justice disempowers politics, reducing its scope for action more and more."
"They are not refugees at all," Schmid reiterates. In the last session, the National Council established that the Maghreb states – Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia – must be considered safe countries of origin. Tens of thousands of unfounded applications, he argues, turn asylum law into a farce: "Once here, it takes a huge effort to expel them."
"Young people need a perspective"
Marc Jost, a National Councillor for the Evangelical People's Party of Switzerland (EVP), also criticizes the current approach: "The events in Ceuta clearly show that the combination of fences and general financial aid does not bring stability." ## Key facts - **What**: Evolution of banking supervision and financial scandals. - When: From 1935 to the present, with a focus on 1965, 1977 and 1984. - Where: Switzerland, with international impact. - Who: CFB, Finma, BNS, SBS, UBS. - Amount: 3 billion francs of support in 1977.
The history of Swiss banking supervision is a tormented one, marked by a constant tension between the need for strict controls and the influence of the financial lobby. The regulatory framework took its first steps after the economic crisis of the 1930s, driven by the bankruptcy of the Banque de Genève in 1931 and the difficulties of the Swiss People's Bank. On March 1, 1935, the Federal Law on Banks and Savings Banks came into force, giving rise to the Federal Commission of Banks (CFB), an independent body in charge of monitoring the liquidity and own funds of institutions.
### The first institutional scandals Trust in the supervisory authority was put to the test as early as the 1960s. On 4 June 1965, the Federal Council decided to dismiss Max Hommel, President of the CFB, with immediate effect. The accusation was serious: Hommel had provided paid advice to companies linked to the Spanish financier Julio Muñoz, involved in the Swiss regulatory developments have often encountered considerable internal resistance, reflecting a political culture that has long debated the appropriateness of stringent state regulation. An emblematic example of this opposition was recorded in May 1984, when a popular initiative aimed at imposing stricter controls on the sector was rejected by the electoral body with 73% of "no" votes. ## In a nutshell - INPS has clarified the changes for the Single and Universal Check. - Extended audience: children residing in another EU State may be entitled. - Specific rules for workers not resident in Italy. - No change for most Italian resident families.
## Key facts - **What**: Circular INPS on Single and Universal Cheque - Where: Italy, with an impact on residents in EU Member States - Who: Community workers and families with children abroad - Date: Application circular published for requests from 21 April 2026 - Requirements: Dependent children according to Italian regulations
The National Institute of Social Security (INPS) has recently published a circular aimed at clarifying the application of the provisions in force regarding the Single and Universal Allowance. This regulatory document is of particular relevance for workers who are nationals of other European Union countries, for families who have tax-dependent children residing in another EU Member State and for all workers who, although carrying out a professional activity in Italy, are not resident in the national territory. The institution's intervention aims to standardise Italian regulations with European directives on the coordination of family benefits, ensuring greater regulatory coherence in cross-border contexts. The most significant update introduced by the recent circular concerns the possibility of including children who reside permanently in another EU member state among the beneficiaries of the Single Allowance. This extension represents a crucial step toward aligning the Italian system with EU principles, allowing those working in Italy to request financial support even when the family unit or part of it is located abroad. However, it remains confirmed that children must be considered fiscally dependent according to Italian regulations to qualify for the benefit. Despite this opening, the calculation of the ISEE remains unchanged: the family unit is determined following existing rules, and the new possibility to include children residing abroad does not alter the structure of the economic indicator.
For non-resident workers providing services in Italy, the circular clearly links the right to the allowance to the period of actual activity carried out on Italian territory. This means that the benefit is conditioned not only on employment status but also on contribution continuity. Those in this situation must pay particular attention to the annual renewal of their application, which must strictly occur between March 1 and February 28 of the following year to cover the annual disbursement cycle. For those without a valid or up-to-date ISEE, INPS confirms the application of the minimum amount, a precautionary measure that ensures a basic economic support while awaiting proper documentation. item.title: Heat on construction sites: SSIC calls for an end to penalties
item.description: The Swiss Society of Manufacturers and Entrepreneurs asks for fair conditions and exemptions from contractual penalties in the event of a stop to the work for the canicola.
item.content:encoded:
IN BRIEF - The SSIC requests the abolition of penalties for delays in construction sites caused by heat. - The heatwave is not considered equivalent to bad weather and lacks compensation. - The Commission of the Council of States considers the parliamentary motion outdated.
KEY FACTS - **What**: Petition for fair conditions in construction sites during heatwaves - When: Parliamentary initiatives between December 2024 and March 2025 - Where: Construction sites throughout Switzerland - Who: Swiss Society of Contractors (SSIC) and Parliament - Amount: Contractual penalties of unspecified amount
During weeks characterized by intense heatwaves, the construction sector in Switzerland faces complex challenges related both to worker safety and to meeting project deadlines. The Swiss Society of Contractors (SSIC) has launched a petition aiming to request the introduction of fair and realistic framework conditions for managing work during extreme temperatures, asking that construction companies are not contractually penalized for the unavoidable delays caused by the heat.
The call for protection and clear rules In the petition, the SSIC emphasizes the urgent need to ensure effective protection of the health of construction workers. Contractors request that realistic deadlines are set for the completion of works and that transparent and uniform rules are established in cases where work must be suspended due to high temperatures.
Unlike what usually happens with adverse weather events or bad weather, interruptions and delays caused by extreme heat are rarely considered in construction contracts. Currently, such circumstances do not benefit from specific compensation, leaving companies exposed to high financial penalties in case of failure to meet agreed deadlines. Since heatwaves cannot be predicted or controlled by either companies or workers, the SSIC considers it unfair to fully burden builders with the economic consequences of these natural events.
Furthermore, the need to adhere to very tight contractual deadlines risks increasing operational pressure on personnel, directly jeopardizing the physical safety of outdoor workers under the blazing sun. Companies seeking to protect their staff by suspending work face potential economic damage related to the enforcement of penalty clauses. To understand the economic context of wages in the sector, it is possible to consult the details on the [Swiss payslip](nav:payslip) and related national parameters. ### The parliamentary framework and the position of the committees
The issue of protection against risks related to extreme temperatures at construction sites has been a topic of discussion within the federal Parliament as well. A pending motion requests the Federal Council to adopt appropriate measures so that natural influences are obligatorily included in planning and executing construction work. The text provides that, in the presence of extreme heat, construction companies should have the option to temporarily suspend activities to protect employees' health, without facing the threat of contractual penalties.
This motion had received support from the National Council, which approved it in December 2024. The parliamentary branch expressed the intention to establish explicit legislative protection for companies and workers.
### The position of the Council of States and the Committee
In March 2025, the Committee for Economics and Taxes of the Council of States announced its opinion on the parliamentary act. While sharing the fundamental objectives related to safeguarding health and ensuring fair working conditions, the Committee pointed out that the situation is already being managed. In line with the position expressed by the federal government, it was clarified that several measures have been initiated within a roundtable involving all relevant social partners in the sector.
Consequently, the Committee recommended that the plenum of the Council of States reject the motion, considering it effectively outdated by ongoing negotiations between employers and workers' representatives. The evolution of the debate highlights how much the issue impacts the [labour market](nav:jobs) and the organization of construction sites in Switzerland.
The discrepancy between the position of the National Council and that of the Committee of the States reflects the complexity of balancing production needs, contractual responsibilities of the client, and the duty to protect workers exposed to severe weather conditions.

The dispute over heatwave management at construction sites highlights the need for companies to carefully assess climate risk management when drafting procurement contracts. In the absence of an official legislative change, the issue remains entrusted to direct contractual negotiations between clients and construction firms, as well as to agreements established within negotiations among social partners.
For construction companies and workers, the immediate priority is to adopt internal preventive measures and adjust working hours during the summer months. Currently discussed practices include reorganizing shifts during the cooler parts of the day, setting up adequate shaded areas, providing refreshing drinks, and temporarily halting the most strenuous tasks when temperatures exceed safety thresholds.
HOW TO PLAN SITE MANAGEMENT AND DEADLINES
To avoid contractual penalties, construction companies planning interventions during the summer months can follow some procedural guidelines:
- Pre-verify contractual clauses related to force majeure events or extraordinary weather influences. - Accurately and promptly document extreme weather conditions detected at the site through official measurements. - Inform project management and clients promptly about the need to suspend activities for health protection reasons. - Stay updated on the outcomes of the social partners' roundtable to incorporate new sector directives as soon as they are defined. - Monitor the economic impact of labor costs on company budgets using the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) tool to assess workforce costs.
The evolution of national negotiations between social partners and institutions will determine whether the recommendations of the SSIC will translate into new regulations or sector-wide binding agreements for all of Switzerland.

## Key facts * **What**: New Frontier Agreement * When: December 23, 2020 * Where: Switzerland * Who: Frontiersmen * Amount: €10,000 (deductible for new frontier workers)
The New Frontier Agreement has been signed to avoid double taxation. Switzerland and Italy already signed the Double Taxation Convention on 9 December 1976.
## What is the New Frontier Agreement The New Frontier Agreement is an agreement between Switzerland and Italy to avoid double taxation of the incomes of frontier workers. This Agreement was signed on 23 December 2020 and enters into force on 1 January 2024.
## Who are the frontiersmen Border workers are people who live in Switzerland and work in Italy, or vice versa. They are subject to a specific tax regime, which provides for the declaration of income both in Switzerland and in Italy.
## How double taxation works Double taxation occurs when a frontier worker is subject to a tax in Switzerland and Italy. For example, if a frontier worker works in Italy and has an income of 50,000 euros, he could be subject to a tax in Italy of 20% and in Switzerland of 10%.
